Point $P$ is where $\theta=\pi$.

These are the formulas for converting from polar coordinates to rectangular (i.e. $x$ and $y$) coordinates:

$\begin{align}
x&=r\cos(\theta)
\\\\
y&=r\sin(\theta)
\end{align}$

[[☃ explanation 1]]

We can use them to obtain an expression for the $x$-coordinate as a function of $\theta$. then we can take the derivative of that expression and evaluate the derivative at $\theta=\pi$.

options.explanation:
In the polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$, the variable $r$ gives the distance from the origin and the variable $\theta$ gives the angle formed with the positive direction of the $x$-axis (in radians).

Using basic trigonometry we can find that the $x$-coordinate of the point $(r,\theta)$ is $r\cos(\theta)$ and the $y$-coordinate is $r\sin(\theta)$.

It starts at the origin and extends to a point on the positive x axis. The other leg of the right triangle, labeled r sine theta, extends upward at a 90 degree angle from this point on the x-axis and ends at a point in the first quadrant. This point in the first quadrant is connected to the origin, creating the hypotenuse of the right triangle, labeled r. The vertex of the right triangle at the origin is labeled theta. hints.content:
Now we can take the derivative of that expression:

$\begin{align}
\dfrac{d}{d\theta}x(\theta)&=\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left[\dfrac15\theta^2\cos(\theta)\right]
\\\\
&=\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac15\theta^2\right)\cdot\cos(\theta)+\dfrac15\theta^2\dfrac{d}{d\theta}[\cos(\theta)]
\\\\
&=\dfrac25\theta\cos(\theta)+\dfrac15\theta^2(-\sin(\theta))
\\\\
&=\dfrac25\theta\cos(\theta)-\dfrac15\theta^2\sin(\theta)
\end{align}$

Now we can plug $\blueD{\theta=\pi}$ into the expression we got:

$\begin{align}
&\phantom{=}\dfrac25(\blueD\pi)\cos(\blueD\pi)-\dfrac15(\blueD\pi)^2\sin(\blueD\pi)
\\\\
&=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}(-1)-\dfrac{\pi^2}{5}(0)
\\\\
&=-\dfrac{2\pi}{5}
\end{align}$

In conclusion, this is the rate of change of the $x$-coordinate with respect to $\theta$ at the point $P$:

$-\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$
